name: PT Argha Karya Prima Industry Tbk

frontmatter.title: Argha Karya Prima — a levered film converter into the feedstock spike
frontmatter.summary: Argha converts imported oil-derived polymer into BOPP, BOPET and CPP packaging film at one Indonesian site, with a Malaysian associate outside the consolidated base. The feedstock spike lifted the spread, but our DCF enterprise value sits below net debt, so the operating business does not cover its borrowings and the equity is worth less than the dividend the model assumes. SELL, target Rp119 against Rp610.
thesis: The market is paying very nearly our bull case: the price puts an enterprise value on the business close to the one the bull scenario produces, while our base case leaves the equity worth less than the dividend the model expects to be paid [S0, S3, S4].

The 2026 margin is a spike, not a level: first-half gross margin was 13.0% against 11.0% for FY2025, 10.3% in FY2024 and 8.3% in FY2023, and no filed note quantifies the mix uplift that would hold it [S2, S3, S4].

The expansion is a wider spread per tonne, not a percentage mark-up: a mark-up on a higher feedstock cost leaves the margin percentage unchanged, so the gain came from the absolute spread and the mix, both of which mean-revert [S3, S5].

The cash flow contradicts the profit: first-half operating cash flow was IDR-146.7bn against net profit of IDR66.2bn, an accruals build of roughly a fifth of total assets, funded by a IDR1,016.6bn short-term loan book that is annually renewable [S3, F35, F39].

Our DCF gives an enterprise value of IDR1,424.5bn, below the net debt on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, so the operating business does not cover its borrowings; the associate at book leaves a sliver of equity, and the target is the bull case discounted by its probability and the liquidity haircut [S4, S3, S0].

blocks.text: **SELL, target Rp119, -63.1% expected total return.** PT Argha Karya Prima Industry Tbk is a converter, not a chemical producer: it buys polypropylene and PET chip, extrudes them into biaxially oriented film at Citeureup in Bogor, and sells the film to food, beverage and consumer-goods packagers [S2]. It consolidates 113,000 tonnes of BOPP capacity, 13,000 tonnes of BOPET and a 7,200 tonne CPP line under construction, a total of 154,200 tonnes less the 21,000 tonnes held through an equity-accounted associate [S2, S3]. The business earned almost nothing for three years, and in 2026 the feedstock spike turned it into a cash machine on the income statement, though not yet in the cash-flow statement [S3].

The variant view is the opposite of the obvious one. The market is not treating the spike as temporary: it is capitalising it. At Rp610 the market capitalisation is IDR373.5bn, which puts an enterprise value on the business close to our bull case, while our DCF says the enterprise is worth about IDR1,424.5bn, below net debt. The difference is not the discount rate and not the terminal growth; it is the terminal margin. The market is paying for a gross margin near the FY2022 peak, while the audited record is 11.0% in FY2025, 10.3% in FY2024 and 8.3% in FY2023 [S2, F32]. We hold the terminal margin at the last audited year, not above it, and what is left for the equity is a sliver that the dividend the model expects would wipe out.

The mechanism matters more than the level. The common explanation, that the company marks up a percentage on a higher feedstock cost, is arithmetically wrong: a percentage mark-up on a higher cost leaves the margin percentage unchanged. What expanded in the first half was the absolute spread per tonne, on a fixed asset base, plus a mix shift toward metallised film [S3, S4]. An absolute spread on a fixed asset base is exactly the item that competition erodes once the feedstock normalises, and it is why we do not carry the first-half level into perpetuity [S5, S3].

The cash flow is the second leg of the call. First-half operating cash flow was a use of IDR-146.7bn, against net profit attributable of IDR66.2bn, because trade receivables rose IDR968.8bn, advances rose IDR56.8bn and the working capital needed to carry a higher-priced inventory and book did not come back [S3, F35, F40, F41]. The company funded that with short-term bank loans of IDR1,016.6bn, up by nearly a third in six months and the majority of gross borrowings [S3]. An equity that needs to fund a working-capital build of this size at annually renewable tenors is not a cheap option on a spread; it is a claim on a residual that the lenders reach first.

Three things move the value, and two of them move it down. First, the terminal spread: it is the whole call, and the engine's own grid shows one point of terminal gross margin taking the twelve-month value from nothing to several times the target, with a point below base already nil (fund record sensitivity grid). Second, the cash conversion: the FY2025 audited accounts show operating cash flow of IDR221.2bn against net profit of IDR12.7bn, which is unusually good, and the first half of 2026 reverses it almost entirely [S4, S3]. Third, the dividend: the company has just approved a payout of about half of FY2024 profit, and we model that ratio rather than a cut, which is the choice the AGM supports and the aggressive one for the balance sheet; at that payout the distribution is larger than the base-case equity value, which is why the twelve-month base case is nil [S2, F20].

The bear case is not a liquidation and the bull case is not a melt-up. The bear is the spread returning to the FY2023 trough while the debt stays on the balance sheet, which floors the equity at zero; the bull is the spread holding at the 2026 level into 2027 with the CPP line ramping, which is roughly where the market trades today [S3, S4]. The base case is the last audited margin on the house Brent deck, and it is the most likely path rather than the cautious one: it assumes the feedstock normalises with the deck, not that it collapses.

Argha was founded in the early years of Indonesia's modern packaging industry and listed on the Jakarta exchange while the domestic food and consumer-goods sectors were still building out. Biaxially oriented polypropylene film is the clear, stiff wrapper used for snacks, biscuits and noodles; biaxially oriented PET film is the heat-resistant cousin used for lidding and electronics; cast polypropylene is the softer film used for laminates. All three are made by melting polymer resin and stretching or casting it into a thin sheet, so the converter's economics are the gap between the resin price and the film price, multiplied by tonnes sold. The industry is capital-intensive at the line level, and a new line takes years to permit, build and qualify with customers.

The company runs one consolidated production site and sells into three product families. At Citeureup in Bogor, West Java, it operates BOPP capacity of 113,000 tonnes a year and BOPET capacity of 13,000 tonnes a year [S2]. A CPP line with capacity of 7,200 tonnes a year was started in 2025 and was still under construction at the annual report date [S2]. Consolidated installed capacity is therefore 113,000 plus 13,000 plus 7,200 tonnes, or 154,200 less the 21,000 tonnes the annual report attributes to Stenta Films in Malaysia [S2]. Stenta is not a subsidiary of the group: the Group holds one eighth of it, the investment is accounted for under the equity method, and the share of its profit is presented on the face of the income statement outside operating profit [S3, note 2g, p6]. The 21,000 tonnes in Malaysia are a real operating asset of a company in which Argha is a minority holder; they are outside the consolidated revenue base and outside the DCF. The product slate includes plain and metallised BOPP, BOPET for lidding and industrial uses, and CPP for laminates; the annual report describes the strategy as moving toward higher-barrier and metallised film rather than commodity plain film [S2].

The customer base is diversified by geography and by account. Export sales were IDR865.2bn of IDR1,754.8bn of first-half 2026 net sales, or just under half, with the balance domestic [S3]. No single customer accounted for more than a tenth of consolidated net sales in either FY2025 or FY2024, which is unusual for an Indonesian converter and a genuine strength [S4]. The company employed 1,006 people at the end of FY2025 [S2]. Sales are made to converters and brand owners in the food, beverage, personal-care and consumer-goods chains, and the film is specified into their packaging lines, which creates a qualification barrier that is more durable than the underlying polymer spread [S2].

The group structure is simple: the listed company owns the Indonesian plant and holds a one-eighth equity-accounted interest in Stenta Films, which contributes its share of profit below the operating line rather than consolidating [S3, S4]. There is no conglomerate overlay and no financial-services arm. The controlling shareholders are PT Tiara Intimahkota with 36.1%, PT Prismatama Nugraha with 27.3% and PT Nawa Panduta with 15.1%, or more than three quarters combined; management holds a small additional stake, and the public holds the balance [S2, F28, F29, F30]. The three holders are related to the founding family and act together, so the company is controlled, but it is not part of a diversified konglo and we do not load the konglo regime [S0, S2].

The business model is a conversion spread. The company buys polymer resin, mostly imported, melts and stretches it, and sells film by the tonne at a price that is negotiated with a lag against the resin price [S4, S6]. Raw materials were IDR1,869.7bn of IDR2,614.9bn of cost of goods sold in FY2025, or about seven tenths of the total, with direct labour and production expenses making up the rest [S4]. The resin is oil-derived: naphtha is the upstream feedstock, and Indonesia imports essentially all of its naphtha, so the cost base is exposed to the oil complex and to the rupiah [S6]. The company's skill is in the film specification, the customer qualification and the speed of the price reset, not in the molecule.

Capital intensity is high and the asset base is old enough to matter. FY2025 capital expenditure was IDR284.4bn of fixed-asset purchases plus IDR62.7bn of advances, a total well above depreciation, because the CPP line and metallising capacity were being built [S4, S2]. Depreciation was IDR164.8bn in FY2025 and IDR153.0bn in FY2024, most of it in production cost [S4]. The plant is therefore being renewed rather than harvested, which is the right choice for a converter with export ambitions but is also why free cash flow is thin at the bottom of the cycle [S4].

The flexible-packaging film industry is a regional price-following business with a handful of large producers and many small converters. Demand grows with food and consumer volumes, which are stable, but supply is lumpy because a new BOPP or BOPET line is a multi-year capital project. The result is a cycle in the film spread that is driven by capacity additions rather than by demand, and the current upcycle is unusual because it is cost-driven: polypropylene rose by more than two fifths year on year by the autumn, and naphtha led it [S5, S6]. A converter that resets its film price quickly earns a wider absolute spread on a higher cost base, but the margin percentage only expands if the absolute gap per tonne widens or the mix improves: a percentage mark-up on a higher resin cost leaves the margin percentage untouched [S3, S4]. The first-half evidence is consistent with a wider absolute spread and a better mix, not with a mark-up, and the distinction is why we treat the first-half margin as cyclical rather than structural [S3].

The policy backdrop has turned supportive, but by less than the headline suggests. The government enacted a finance-minister regulation in October 2026 granting a zero per cent import duty on six polymer tariff lines for six months, explicitly to ease feedstock costs for the domestic plastics industry [S5]. Two caveats come from the same article: it states that the imports covered are currently mostly liquid forms rather than the polymer pellets a film converter buys, and it does not publish the pre-relief duty rate [S5]. We therefore cannot turn the regulation into a point estimate of saving, and we do not: each percentage point of duty on the imported polymer share is worth about one part in seventy-five of gross profit, a rounding item against a target that turns on the terminal margin, and the extension is carried in the bull narrative rather than in the base [S4, S5, F15]. The risk is that it expires: a six-month window means the benefit is temporary, and the industry's cost advantage reverses when the duty returns unless the polymer price moves in its favour [S5].

Competition is regional. The large integrated producers in Thailand, Malaysia and China make film and resin, and they can undercut a non-integrated Indonesian converter when resin is cheap and the rupiah is strong [S6]. Argha's defence is customer qualification, metallising capability and the Malaysian plant's access to regional customers, not low cost [S2]. The company is a challenger to the integrated regional producers in commodity film and a genuine specialist in metallised and high-barrier film, where the qualification cycle is longer and the price is stickier [S2]. That mix is why the gross margin held in the spike: commodity film is a pass-through, but metallised film carries a specification premium.

The moat is narrow but real. A new entrant needs a line, a customer qualification and a film formulation, which takes years; the installed base of BOPP lines in the region is concentrated among a few producers [S2, S6]. Against that, the company has no feedstock integration, imports its resin, and competes with producers that make their own polymer. Supplier power is therefore high and buyer power is moderate: no customer is above a tenth of sales, but the large brand owners can qualify a second source [S4]. The threat of substitutes is low for food packaging, because the film is the package, and rivalry is price-based in commodity grades and specification-based in metallised grades [S2].

The house decks put numbers on the cost side. Brent runs from US$98.3/bbl spot to US$96.0/bbl in FY2026E and US$84.0/bbl in FY2027E, a fall of about an eighth, which is the single most important external variable for the spread [S4]. The rupiah matters too: the macro deck carries the exchange rate at Rp18,350/USD against a spot of Rp18,103/USD, and a weaker rupiah raises the landed cost of imported resin for a company that earns a large share of revenue in dollars [S6]. The oil and currency effects partly offset, which is why we model the spread directly rather than a dollar cost pass-through.

The history is a converter that lost its spread in the downcycle and has now recovered it. Revenue was IDR3,105.6bn in FY2022, fell to IDR2,723.6bn in FY2023, recovered to IDR3,025.0bn and was IDR2,938.7bn in FY2025 [S0, S4]. Gross profit went from IDR375.0bn to IDR225.0bn and then to IDR323.8bn, a gross margin of 11.0% [S4, S2]. Operating profit collapsed to IDR16.1bn in FY2023 and recovered to IDR97.7bn in FY2025, still below the FY2022 level [S0, S4]. The swing is the spread, not volume: revenue moved by less than a fifth across those years while operating profit moved by a multiple [S4].

The first half of 2026 is the inflection. Revenue was IDR1,754.8bn against a prior-year comparative that was about a fifth lower, gross profit was IDR228.4bn, operating profit was IDR129.9bn and net profit was IDR66.2bn against a loss [S3]. The driver is visible in the feedstock market: polypropylene rose by more than two fifths year on year by mid-October 2026 and naphtha led it, so the resin price rose and the film price followed [S5, S6]. What the accounts do not support is the report's earlier claim that a percentage mark-up lifted the margin: a mark-up on a higher cost leaves the margin percentage unchanged. The gross margin expanded by nearly three points because the absolute spread per tonne widened and the mix moved toward metallised film, and both of those are cyclical in a business with no feedstock integration [S3, S4].

The accounts need one restatement before they can be used. The data pack carries depreciation of IDR164.8bn for FY2025, which is only a fragment of the charge; the fixed-asset note shows IDR164.8bn in FY2025 and IDR153.0bn in FY2024, split between production cost, general and administrative expense and selling expense [S4]. The pack's operating profit is also low: the audited income statement shows IDR97.7bn for FY2025 and IDR110.4bn for FY2024, against the pack's lower figures [S4]. We restate both lines from the filing. The restatement turns EBITDA from a number close to operating profit into a number close to operating profit plus the depreciation charge, and it is the correct base for the leverage and coverage discussion [S4].

Our forecast follows the last actual and the house deck. FY2026E revenue is IDR3,497.1bn, a growth rate of 19.0%, because the first half is already booked and the second half is set at the first-half run-rate rather than at the stronger second quarter [S3]. FY2027E falls -6.0% as Brent normalises from US$96.0/bbl to US$84.0/bbl and the selling price deflates with the resin cost, partly offset by volume from the CPP line [S4, S2]. FY2028E grows 3.0% and the later years 4.0% a year, which is Indonesian packaging demand plus the CPP ramp, and the terminal rate is 4.0% [S2, S0].

Margins are calibrated to the first half, then anchored on the last audited year. The gross-margin input is 14.3% at FY2025 input costs, which the model's Brent link takes to a reported 13.0%, reproducing the IDR228.4bn on IDR1,754.8bn first-half print [S3, S4]. That is a four-point calibration gap against the FY2025 audited EBITDA margin of under nine per cent, and we state it rather than bury it: the following year that ignored a booked half of IDR129.9bn of operating profit would be ignoring the only sourced evidence in the file [S3, F12]. From FY2027E the reported margin is 12.5% and it settles at about 11.0% in the terminal year, which is the FY2025 audited 11.0% and below the FY2022 peak; no filed note quantifies a mix uplift, so the base case carries none [S2, F32, S4]. SG&A is 5.6% of revenue in FY2026E, reproducing the reported first-half operating profit, and drifts to 6.2% as revenue deflates against a largely fixed cost base [S3, S4].

The cash flow is where the leverage shows. Operating profit is IDR260.4bn and EBITDA IDR452.7bn, but capital expenditure is 3.9% of revenue, the first-half cash run-rate, and working capital absorbs 32.8% of the higher revenue [S4, S3]. Free cash flow is therefore IDR68.4bn in FY2026E and IDR223.4bn in FY2027E, positive but well below the profit, because the working-capital number carried on a revenue base up 19.0% takes most of the gain [S4]. The forecast is not a liquidity crisis, but it does show that the 2026 profit does not all reach the balance sheet: the June borrowing increase is the evidence [S3].

The balance sheet is levered and the maturity is short. At the end of FY2025 debt was IDR1,340.7bn, cash was IDR78.4bn, and equity was IDR1,777.0bn [S4, S0]; the June 2026 LK shows borrowing higher again after the working-capital build [S3]. Finance expense was IDR70.2bn in FY2025 and the first-half 2026 run-rate is similar, against operating profit of IDR129.9bn in the half, so interest cover is comfortable while the spread holds [S4, S3]. The structure is the problem, not the cover: short-term bank loans were IDR1,016.6bn at 30 June 2026, up by nearly a third in six months and nearly two thirds of gross borrowings, against cash, restricted funds pledged on the facilities and short-term investments that together are a fraction of the maturing lines [S3]. The dividend is the appropriation of FY2024 profit: Rp8 a share, paid during 2025 and equal to just under half of FY2024 net profit, and no FY2025 dividend had been resolved at the annual report date [S2, p79, F20]. We model that payout ratio going forward because it is the only one the company has approved, and the balance sheet carries the difference [S2, S4].

Earnings quality, run through the house screens, is now the second leg of the call. The 2026 profit is operating, not below the line: there is no fair-value gain carrying the result, and the associate contribution of IDR4.4bn is presented outside operating profit [S3]. The cash flow is printed in the filing and it does not support the profit. Net cash provided by operating activities was IDR208.1bn in FY2024 and IDR221.2bn in FY2025 on net profit of IDR10.6bn and IDR12.7bn, an accruals ratio of about minus six per cent of average total assets in each year: earnings were cash-backed and then some [S4, p19]. In the first half of 2026 the sign reverses: operating cash flow was a use of IDR-146.7bn against net profit attributable of IDR66.2bn, an accruals ratio of about plus five and a half per cent of average total assets, because trade receivables rose to IDR968.8bn from a year-end level more than half as low again, and advances rose to IDR56.8bn from almost nothing [S3, p4 and p9]. The forecast carries the working-capital intensity the actual shows, at the FY2025 ratio of net working capital to revenue, rather than assuming a release in the one year the filing shows the opposite [S4, S3]. Customer concentration is low, related-party sales are a rounding item, and we found no special notation, material legal case or administrative sanction in the annual report [S2, S4]. The free float is thin, which is a liquidity flag rather than an accounting one [S0].

We value Argha on a discounted cash flow of the operating business. The method fits because the multiples are distorted by the cycle in opposite directions: the trailing PE of 29.5x uses trough earnings, while the forward PE of 2.7x uses a spike year, and neither is a through-cycle number [S0, S3]. The DCF uses the full forecast, including the feedstock normalisation in FY2027E, and it is the only method that captures the leverage explicitly through net debt [S4].

The discount rate is the house build with one correction, and the correction has a second effect we disclose. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, the country risk premium 2.5%, and the industry unlevered beta 0.90; at the capped debt-to-equity ratio of 2.00 the levered beta is 2.30, giving a cost of equity of 15.5% and a WACC of 10.1% [S4]. The correction is to the cost of debt: the engine prices it at the risk-free rate plus the corporate spread, or 9.4%, while the company actually pays about 5.8% on its bank facilities, most of which are US dollar trade lines priced at five to seven per cent, and the Company's functional currency is the dollar, so the rupiah risk-free rate is not the relevant base [S4, S3, note 16]. Because debt is two thirds of the capital structure at the cap, that gap overstates WACC by about two percentage points; we offset it through the cost of equity rather than by editing the deck, and the note in the assumptions file sets out the arithmetic [S4]. The second effect is that the same cost of equity rolls the twelve-month target forward, so the correction also lowers the roll factor from about one and twenty-one hundredths to one and fifteen hundredths. We disclose the direction rather than claim the higher figure an unadjusted roll would give, and we note that a cost of equity near sixteen per cent is the low end of defensible for a two-thirds debt-funded, thin-float converter [S4, S3].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR1,424.5bn against the 30 June 2026 balance sheet: short-term bank loans of IDR1,016.6bn, current maturities of long-term borrowings of IDR21.8bn and long-term borrowings of IDR528.4bn, less cash on hand and in banks of IDR65.2bn and short-term investments of IDR12.8bn [S3]. The operating business therefore comes in below its net debt, so the borrowings are not covered by the enterprise value and the equity is a residual on the associate: adding IDR100.4bn of book value turns the deficit into a small positive equity value of Rp59 a share, and rolling that forward at the cost of equity and paying the dividend the model expects leaves the twelve-month base case at Rp0 against a price of Rp610 [S3, F37, S0]. This is not a rounding error dressed up as a view; it is what a business whose enterprise value is below net debt looks like. The terminal value carries about half the enterprise value, which is normal for a going concern but is also the point of sensitivity: the value depends on the terminal spread, and we hold it at the FY2025 audited level rather than at the 2026 peak [S4]. Free cash flow is IDR68.4bn in FY2026E, IDR223.4bn in FY2027E and about IDR106.2bn in FY2028E, so the value is back-end loaded and a higher discount rate hurts it disproportionately [S4].

The capex path is set by the only current evidence, not by a convention. First-half 2026 capex was IDR45.3bn of fixed-asset acquisitions plus IDR22.8bn of advances for fixed-asset purchases [S3, p9], a run-rate of 3.9% of revenue, and we hold that for the year rather than assuming a second-half step-up that no filing schedules: the fixed-asset note says only that the advances went to several suppliers for machinery, equipment and construction services, and the annual report says the CPP line is still under construction without giving a completion date [S3, note 14, S2]. From FY2027E capex is 5.5% of revenue, the restated depreciation rate, so the terminal year reinvests exactly what it consumes; with no disclosed second project we do not assume another line, and we do not assume the first-half rate persists for ever either, because a company growing at 4.0% nominal has to replace what it wears out [S4, F8, S2].

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is the finding. On EV/EBITDA the stock is at 3.6x our FY2026E EBITDA and 4.0x FY2027E, and on price-to-book at 0.2x reported book [S0, S3]. The book multiple is the one that needs care, because the reported book is not the shareholders' clean figure: equity attributable to owners was IDR1,936.0bn at 30 June 2026 and the exchange-rate translation reserve within it was IDR534.7bn, so equity excluding the reserve is about one and four tenths trillion rupiah and the P/B on clean equity is nearer three tenths than two [S3, F42, F43]. That reserve is real but reversible: a five per cent appreciation of the rupiah against the dollar and the Hong Kong dollar would reverse about a twentieth of it, because the Company's functional currency is the dollar and the reporting currency the rupiah [S4, note 2]. The engine's multiple methods use FY2025 trailing earnings, which are the trough, so they produce a trough multiple and a floored zero on EV/EBITDA; we give them no weight for that reason [S4, S3]. The DCF is the primary method, and the forward EV/EBITDA cross-check says the market is paying our bull case, not our base case [S0].

The sensitivity grid is the map of the risk, and it is steeper than a target of Rp119 suggests. Half a point on the WACC takes the base value from Rp59 a share to nothing, and a point lower takes it to several times that, because the enterprise value sits below net debt and the equity is a thin sliver; a point of terminal growth moves it by a similar order. The gross margin is steeper still: one point above base takes the twelve-month value to several times the target and two points to more than ten times it, while a point below base is already nil (fund record sensitivity grids;
). The margin is therefore not a light sensitivity to be noted and set aside: the call turns on roughly one point of terminal gross margin, and that is where the scenario analysis belongs [S3, S2].

What the price implies. The engine's reverse DCF does not bracket this name, because the value responds to the revenue-growth driver through the terminal value and the leverage in a way that is not monotonic at the endpoints, so we decompose the gap on the balance sheet instead [S4]. At Rp610 the market capitalisation is IDR373.5bn; adding the gross borrowings on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet — short-term bank loans of IDR1,016.6bn, current maturities of IDR21.8bn and long-term borrowings of IDR528.4bn — and deducting cash on hand and in banks of IDR65.2bn and short-term investments of IDR12.8bn gives an enterprise value of about one and nine tenths trillion rupiah, or about one and three quarter trillion net of the IDR100.4bn associate [S0, S3, F37]. Against the DCF enterprise value of IDR1,424.5bn the market is roughly a quarter above our number, not close to it. The reverse arithmetic gives the same answer as the forward one: to justify the price on our forecast the terminal reported gross margin would have to sit at or above the FY2022 peak, which is precisely the margin the market is paying for and precisely the one no filed note supports [S2, F32, S4].

The scenario values frame the answer, and the decomposition is the argument. Our base case is Rp0 at half the weight, the bear case Rp0 at three tenths and the bull case Rp743 at a fifth, which weights to a value before the house liquidity discount of about Rp149 and a target of Rp119 [S0, S4]. Read that decomposition carefully: the entire target is the bull case. The bear leaves nothing because the enterprise value falls below net debt; the base leaves nothing at twelve months because the equity value of Rp59 a share is smaller than the dividend the model expects to be paid, so the roll-forward nets to nil. The asymmetry is the leverage, not a modelling artefact. It is what a company with net debt several times its market value looks like when the spread normalises, and it is why the rating is not sensitive to the probability weights: at a fifth of the weight on the bull the target is a small fraction of the price, and at a quarter it is still a small fraction of the price [S3, S4]. The bull case is close to where the stock trades today — the price implies an enterprise value within a twentieth of the bull case's — which is the cleanest statement of the call we can make [S0, S3].

**Feedstock reversal (high likelihood, high impact).** The company's margin is a mark-up on a polymer price that is set by naphtha, and naphtha rose by almost all of its value in the year to the autumn [S6]. If the resin price falls faster than the film price, the mark-up compresses and the gross margin returns to the FY2024-FY2025 level of about a tenth [S4]. The first-half evidence says the pass-through is fast, but the second half is the test, and a single quarter of mismatch would take a large bite out of the year [S3].

**Leverage and refinancing (medium likelihood, high impact).** Net debt is several times the market capitalisation, and the debt is overwhelmingly short-dated: IDR1,016.6bn of short-term bank loans at 30 June 2026, nearly two thirds of gross borrowings, up by nearly a third in six months, against cash, restricted funds and short-term investments that together do not cover it [S3, p5]. The facilities are annually renewable trade finance, so the roll is the event. A rise in the BI rate, a tightening of bank liquidity or a further working-capital swing would hit the equity before it hit the operating business, and the June borrowing increase shows that the cycle can consume cash even while it produces profit [S3]. We hold gross debt flat in the forecast rather than assuming repayment, because a repayment slope is not disclosed and would not be funded by free cash flow after a half-of-profit dividend [S3, S4, F20]. The bear case is where the repricing sits: a two-hundred-basis-point increase on the short-term book is about a tenth of FY2026E operating profit, which is small against the equity and large against the residual after net debt [S3, S4].

**Demand and export exposure (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Just under half of first-half sales were exports [S3]. A weaker global consumer, a stronger rupiah or a regional recession would reduce volume and mix, and the Malaysian plant's sales are exposed to the same cycle [S2]. The customer base is diversified, which limits the damage from any one account, but it does not protect against a regional downturn [S4].

**Capacity execution (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The CPP line is under construction, and a delay or a cost overrun would push out the volume and the margin mix that the forecast assumes [S2]. The line is small relative to the group, so the impact is modest, but it is the only growth capex in the plan and a failure would leave the company with a flat volume base [S2, S4].

**Policy (medium likelihood, medium impact, two-sided).** The zero import duty on certain plastic raw materials runs for six months [S5]. Its expiry raises landed feedstock cost unless the government extends it, and its extension would be a positive surprise. The policy is explicitly a response to the feedstock spike, so it is likely to be extended while the spike lasts and to lapse when it does [S5].

**Governance and related parties (low likelihood, medium impact).** The three controlling holders own most of the shares, the public float is thin, and the company transacts with related parties at the margin [S2]. We found no improper transaction, but a related-party deal or a capital action that favours the controlling group would be the route by which minority value is transferred [S2, S4].

**Liquidity (high likelihood, medium impact).** The stock trades IDR465.5m a day, and the free float is less than a fifth of the shares [S0]. We apply the house liquidity discount to the target; an investor who needs to exit quickly will do worse than the screen price [S0].

**Currency (medium likelihood, low impact).** Revenue is partly dollar-linked and resin is imported, so the rupiah affects both sides. The net effect is modest because the company passes the cost through, but a sharp move would show up in working capital and in the translation of the Malaysian associate [S3, S6].

The bear case returns the gross margin to the FY2023 trough and takes revenue growth four points below base in every year, which is the spread normalising faster than the deck assumes while the debt stays on the balance sheet [S4, S3]. Its equity is floored at zero because the enterprise value falls below net debt, not because the company is insolvent: the assets and the customer base remain, but the residual for shareholders is negative before the floor, which is what separates it from the base [S3]. The base case is the FY2025 audited margin on the house deck: it leaves Rp59 a share before the dividend, less than the distribution the model assumes, so the twelve-month value is Rp0 [S3, S4]. The bull case holds the spread at the 2026 level into 2027, adds a point and a half of margin from mix, and runs revenue four points above base as the CPP line ramps; the equity re-rates sharply because the operating leverage is high and the debt is fixed [S2, S3]. The shocks are mirrored at four points of growth and a point and a half of margin, and the probabilities give the base half the weight, the bear three tenths and the bull a fifth, because the first-half evidence supports a good FY2026 but the cash-flow statement and the maturity wall make the bear at least as likely as the bull [S3, S4].

The signposts that would change our view, in order: the third-quarter gross margin, which tells us whether the pass-through held after the June peak; the net-debt trajectory, which tells us whether the cycle is consuming cash; the CPP line start-up, which tells us whether the mix shift is real; the extension or expiry of the import-duty relief; and any related-party or capital action [S3, S5, S2].

Ownership is concentrated and stable. PT Tiara Intimahkota holds 36.1%, PT Prismatama Nugraha 27.3% and PT Nawa Panduta 15.1%, with management holding a small additional stake and the public holding the balance [S2]. The three holders are related to the founding family and act together, so the company is controlled; the free float is less than a fifth of the shares and the stock trades IDR465.5m a day [S0, S2]. The practical consequence is that minority holders have little influence over capital allocation, and the debt and dividend decisions are made by the controlling group [S2].

Related-party dealings are small in the trading line. Sales to related parties were a rounding item of first-half revenue, and the annual report discloses no material related-party purchase or asset transaction [S3, S4]. The group's associate contributes a small share of profit and is consolidated by the equity method [S4]. We found no pledged-share disclosure, no material legal case, no administrative sanction and no special notation in the annual report or the half-year LK [S2, S3]. The auditor is the Indonesian member firm of EY, which issued an unqualified opinion on the FY2025 accounts [S4]. We found no auditor change, qualification or restatement in the period we reviewed [S4].

The dividend record is real but it is a distribution of the prior year's profit, not a policy. The annual general meeting appropriated FY2024 net profit and paid Rp8 a share during 2025, equal to just under half of FY2024 profit attributable to owners; no FY2025 dividend had been resolved at the annual report date [S2, p79, F20]. We model that approved ratio going forward rather than a cut, because a cut would be a judgment with no company guidance behind it, and the balance sheet carries the difference: at that payout the FY2026E distribution is about Rp106 a share, more than the base-case equity value per share, so the dividend is paid out of a business that the model says is worth less than the distribution [S4, S3]. The dividend is not the reason to own the stock, and at this leverage it is a reason not to: the cash leaves the company in the year the working capital needs it [S3].

On ESG, the exposures are those of a polymer converter: energy use in the extrusion lines, solvent handling in the metallising and printing processes, and the end-of-life profile of plastic packaging, which is the industry's central regulatory risk [S2]. The company reports no material environmental sanction and no material legal case in the annual report, and its product strategy is toward higher-barrier and metallised film rather than thicker commodity film, which is a modest positive for material intensity [S2]. The governance score is held back less by any single finding than by the combination of a controlling group, a thin free float and a leveraged balance sheet that limits minority influence over capital allocation [S2, S0].

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. The nearest is the third-quarter 2026 financial statements, expected in the current quarter, which will show whether the gross margin held after the June peak and whether the borrowing increase reversed [S3]. The FY2026 audited results follow in the first quarter of 2027, with the dividend proposal; the annual general meeting follows in the second quarter [S2, S4]. The CPP line is still under construction and the company discloses no completion date, so its start-up announcement, not a date in the diary, is the first read on the mix shift that the forecast assumes [S2].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are these. First, the gross margin, which is the spread and the whole operating model; we track it quarterly because it moved from the FY2025 level to the first-half 2026 level in two quarters [S4, S3]. Second, the ratio of revenue to raw-material cost, which tells us whether the pass-through is holding or the mark-up is compressing [S3, S4]. Third, net debt and interest cover, which tell us whether the cycle is producing cash or consuming it [S3]. Fourth, the export share, which tells us whether the regional demand is holding [S3]. Fifth, the CPP line progress and the metallising mix, which tell us whether the margin uplift is structural [S2]. Sixth, the import-duty relief and any change in the oil or rupiah decks, which set the feedstock cost [S5, S4].

What would make us wrong on the upside: the feedstock spike persisting into 2027, a faster CPP ramp, a stronger export market, or an extension of the import-duty relief that lowers the landed resin cost [S5, S6]. What would make us wrong on the downside: a sharp fall in the film price relative to resin, a refinancing squeeze, or a related-party use of cash that minority holders do not share in [S3, S2]. We would revisit the rating on any of these, and on the third-quarter accounts.
